# Introduction

## Purpose of the Assignment

This study note documents my work through the UCLA seminar *Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) in R with lavaan*. I coded along with the seminar using the SAQ-8 questionnaire, and I explain what each analysis does, why it is run, what the output means, and what conclusion follows. The goal is a reference I can reuse when conducting or reviewing a CFA.

## Confirmatory Factor Analysis and Exploratory Factor Analysis

Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) lets the data suggest how many factors there are and which items load on which factors. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) is the opposite: I specify the number of factors and which items load on each factor *before* looking at the data, then test how well that theory reproduces the observed covariances. CFA is therefore theory-driven and testable, while EFA is data-driven.

# Data and Software

## Required Packages

```{r}
# haven reads SPSS (.sav) files; lavaan fits CFA / SEM models
library(haven)
library(lavaan)
```

## Importing the SAQ-8 Data

```{r}
# The seminar reads this file with foreign::read.spss(..., use.value.labels = FALSE).
# The assignment installs haven, so I read the same UCLA file (SAQ.sav) with haven::read_sav().
# download.file() comes first because it follows redirects from UCLA's old address.
# TODO (Cecilia): if the download fails, save SAQ.sav from the UCLA seminar page next to
# this .qmd and replace the three download lines with: dat <- read_sav("SAQ.sav")
url <- "https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/SAQ.sav"
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".sav")
download.file(url, tmp, mode = "wb")
dat <- read_sav(tmp)

# Drop the SPSS value labels so every item is a plain number (the seminar's
# use.value.labels = FALSE does the same). The file has 23 variables; q01-q08 come first.
dat <- as.data.frame(zap_labels(dat))
```

## Examining the Data

```{r}
# Structure: variable names, types, and labels
str(dat)

# First several observations
head(dat)

# Sample size
nrow(dat)
```

```{r}
# Covariance and correlation matrices for the 8 items
items <- paste0("q0", 1:8)
round(cov(dat[, items]), 2)
round(cor(dat[, items]), 2)
```

**Interpretation.** The correlation matrix shows how strongly each pair of items moves together. Items that correlate substantially with one another are candidates to share a common latent factor. Items with weak correlations to the rest (check q02 in your output) are likely poor indicators of a general factor.
The correlated two-factor model appears most appropriate: it fits far better than the one-factor and uncorrelated two-factor models (CFI = [your CFI], RMSEA = [your RMSEA]), and the factors correlate at [your factor correlation], so treating them as unrelated is not supported. However, the second-order model has identical fit, so the choice between them rests on theory, and because q02 was dropped after looking at the data, the structure should be cross-validated on a new sample before it is treated as final.

# CFA Concepts

## Observed Indicators and Latent Factors

In the SAQ-8, the **observed indicators** are the eight questionnaire items (q01–q08), each rated on a Likert scale. The **latent factor(s)** are the unobserved construct(s) the items are assumed to measure, here statistics anxiety. Factor loadings link each item to its factor.

| Item | Wording (rated 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) |
|---|---|
| q01 | Statistics makes me cry |
| q02 | My friends will think I'm stupid for not being able to cope with SPSS |
| q03 | Standard deviations excite me |
| q04 | I dream that Pearson is attacking me with correlation coefficients |
| q05 | I don't understand statistics |
| q06 | I have little experience with computers |
| q07 | All computers hate me |
| q08 | I have never been good at mathematics |

The full data file has 23 variables; this note uses only q01–q08 (N = 2571 in the seminar).

## The Measurement Model

For item *i* and person *j*:

$$x_{ij} = \tau_i + \lambda_i \eta_j + \varepsilon_{ij}$$

- $\lambda_i$ is the **factor loading**: how much the item changes per unit change in the factor.
- $\eta_j$ is the person's latent factor score.
- $\varepsilon_{ij}$ is the **residual** (unique variance): item variance not explained by the factor, including measurement error.

## The Model-Implied Covariance Matrix

The model implies $\Sigma(\theta) = \Lambda \Psi \Lambda' + \Theta$, where $\Lambda$ holds loadings, $\Psi$ is the factor (co)variance, and $\Theta$ is the residual covariance matrix. CFA estimates the parameters so that $\Sigma(\theta)$ is as close as possible to the observed sample covariance matrix. Fit statistics measure how close that is.

## Path Diagrams

In a path diagram, ovals are latent factors, rectangles are observed items, single-headed arrows are loadings, and small arrows pointing into items are residuals.

## Model Identification and Degrees of Freedom

- **Known values:** the unique variances and covariances in the sample matrix, $p(p+1)/2$ for $p$ items.
- **Free parameters:** values the model estimates (loadings, residual variances, factor variance).
- **Fixed parameters:** values set by the analyst (e.g., a loading fixed to 1, residual covariances fixed to 0).
- **Degrees of freedom** = known values − free parameters.

| Model status | df | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Under-identified | < 0 | More unknowns than knowns; cannot be estimated |
| Just-identified (saturated) | = 0 | Fits perfectly by construction; fit cannot be tested |
| Over-identified | > 0 | Testable; fit statistics are meaningful |

**Three-item example.** With 3 items there are $3(4)/2 = 6$ known values. The model needs 3 loadings, 3 residual variances, and 1 factor variance = 7 parameters, which is too many. Fixing one loading to 1 (marker method) or fixing the factor variance to 1 (variance standardization) removes one, leaving 6 free parameters. df = 6 − 6 = 0, so the model is just-identified.

# One-Factor CFA

## Three-Item Model

```{r}
# Marker-variable method: lavaan fixes the first loading (q03) to 1
m1a <- 'f =~ q03 + q04 + q05'
fit1a <- cfa(m1a, data = dat)
summary(fit1a, standardized = TRUE)
```

```{r}
# Variance-standardization method: free the first loading (NA*),
# fix the factor variance to 1
m1b <- '
  f =~ NA*q03 + q04 + q05
  f ~~ 1*f
'
fit1b <- cfa(m1b, data = dat)
summary(fit1b, standardized = TRUE)
```

## Model Specification

`f =~ q03 + q04 + q05` reads as "the latent factor **f** is *measured by* q03, q04, and q05." The `=~` operator defines a latent variable from its indicators. By default lavaan fixes the first loading to 1 (marker method) and estimates the others.

**Marker vs. variance standardization.** The marker method sets the scale of the factor to match one item (loading = 1) and estimates the factor variance. The variance-standardization method sets the factor variance to 1 and estimates every loading. Both are equally identified, use the same number of free parameters, and give identical fit; only the parameter scaling differs. The *standardized* solution is the same under both.

## Standardized Solution

```{r}
standardizedSolution(fit1a)

# Model-implied covariance matrix vs. observed
fitted(fit1a)
inspect(fit1a, "sample")
```

## Eight-Item Model

```{r}
m2 <- 'f =~ q01 + q02 + q03 + q04 + q05 + q06 + q07 + q08'
# std.lv = TRUE = variance-standardization method (factor variance fixed to 1), as in the seminar
fit2 <- cfa(m2, data = dat, std.lv = TRUE)
summary(fit2, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
```

## Model-Fit Statistics

```{r}
fitMeasures(fit2, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr"))
```

| Statistic | What it tells you | Common guideline |
|---|---|---|
| Chi-square | Exact-fit test of model vs. data; sensitive to sample size | Non-significant p is ideal, but large samples nearly always reject |
| CFI | Improvement over a null (no-relationships) model | ≥ .95 good (≥ .90 acceptable) |
| TLI | Like CFI, with a penalty for complexity | About ≥ .90 (seminar); ≥ .95 is stricter |
| RMSEA | Misfit per degree of freedom | Seminar guideline: ≤ .05 close fit; .05–.08 acceptable; ≥ .10 poor |
| SRMR | Average residual correlation | ≤ .08 good |

## Uncorrelated Factors

The seminar drops q02 (weakest loading, about -.23) and splits the remaining seven items into two factors: **f1** (q01, q03, q04, q05, q08) is called SPSS Anxiety, and **f2** (q06, q07) is called Attribution Bias.

```{r}
# Orthogonal = factors forced to be uncorrelated.
# f2 has only two items. With no correlation to f1 to help, the model is identified by
# equating the two f2 loadings (label "a") and fixing the factor variances to 1 (std.lv = TRUE).
m3a <- '
  f1 =~ q01 + q03 + q04 + q05 + q08
  f2 =~ a*q06 + a*q07
  f1 ~~ 0*f2
'
fit3a <- cfa(m3a, data = dat, std.lv = TRUE)
summary(fit3a, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
```

## Correlated Factors

```{r}
# Oblique = factors allowed to correlate (lavaan's default).
# Now the two-item factor f2 is identified through its covariance with f1,
# so the two q06/q07 loadings no longer need to be equal.
m3b <- '
  f1 =~ q01 + q03 + q04 + q05 + q08
  f2 =~ q06 + q07
'
fit3b <- cfa(m3b, data = dat, std.lv = TRUE)
summary(fit3b, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
```

## Model Comparison

```{r}
# Compare fit across models (the models must use the same items for anova())
fitMeasures(fit3a, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea"))
fitMeasures(fit3b, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea"))
anova(fit3a, fit3b)
```

# Second-Order CFA

## Model Specification

```{r}
# Second-order factor f3 ("overall anxiety") explains why f1 and f2 are correlated.
# Seminar's marker-method version: both second-order loadings fixed to 1, f3 variance estimated.
m4a <- '
  f1 =~ q01 + q03 + q04 + q05 + q08
  f2 =~ q06 + q07
  f3 =~ 1*f1 + 1*f2
  f3 ~~ f3
'
fit4a <- cfa(m4a, data = dat)
summary(fit4a, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

# Seminar's variance-standardization version: f3 variance fixed to 1 and the two
# second-order loadings constrained equal. The chi-square and df must match fit4a.
m4b <- '
  f1 =~ NA*q01 + q03 + q04 + q05 + q08
  f2 =~ NA*q06 + q07
  f3 =~ NA*f1 + equal("f3=~f1")*f2
  f1 ~~ 1*f1
  f2 ~~ 1*f2
  f3 ~~ 1*f3
'
fit4b <- cfa(m4b, data = dat)
fitMeasures(fit4a, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr"))
fitMeasures(fit4b, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr"))
```

## Interpretation

A second-order factor represents a broader general construct (e.g., overall statistics anxiety) that accounts for the correlations among the narrower first-order factors. With only two first-order factors, the second-order factor can be identified only by adding a constraint (here, both second-order loadings fixed to 1, or set equal). The result is a model that is statistically equivalent to the correlated two-factor model: it has the same chi-square and degrees of freedom. Fit therefore cannot choose between the two, and the choice has to rest on theory.

# Practice Questions and Answers
**1. What is the difference between EFA and CFA?**
EFA discovers the factor structure from the data; CFA tests a structure specified in advance.

**2. What are the observed indicators and latent factors in the SAQ-8?**
Indicators: items q01–q08. Latent factor(s): statistics anxiety (one general factor, or sub-factors in the two-factor and second-order models).

**3. What do factor loadings represent?**
The strength of the relationship between a factor and an item. Standardized loadings are interpreted like regression coefficients on standardized variables.

**4. What do residual variances represent?**
Item variance not explained by the factor (unique variance plus measurement error).

**5. How many unique variances and covariances are available for three indicators?**
$3(3+1)/2 = 6$.

**6. Fixed vs. free parameter?**
A fixed parameter is set by the analyst to a constant; a free parameter is estimated from the data.

**7. Why is a model with negative df under-identified?**
There are more parameters to estimate than known pieces of information, so there is no unique solution.

**8. Why does fixing one loading and setting residual covariances to zero help identification?**
For three items the model-implied covariance matrix has 10 unique parameters (3 loadings, 1 factor variance, 6 residual variances and covariances) but only 6 known values. Fixing one loading to 1 (marker method) and the 3 residual covariances to 0 removes 4, leaving 10 - 4 = 6 free parameters, so df = 6 - 6 = 0 and the model is just-identified.

**9. Just-identified vs. over-identified?**
Just-identified: df = 0, perfect fit by construction. Over-identified: df > 0, so the fit can be tested.

**10. How are chi-square, CFI, TLI, and RMSEA interpreted?**
See the table in the one-factor section: judge them together, not individually.

**11. Correlated vs. uncorrelated factors?**
Uncorrelated factors are constrained to covary 0; correlated factors have the covariance freely estimated.

**12. What does a second-order factor represent?**
A general construct that explains the correlations among first-order factors.

**13. Which model appears most appropriate?**
The correlated two-factor model appears most appropriate: it fits far better than the one-factor and uncorrelated two-factor models (CFI = [your CFI], RMSEA = [your RMSEA]), and the factors correlate at [your factor correlation], so treating them as unrelated is not supported. However, the second-order model has identical fit, so the choice between them rests on theory, and because q02 was dropped after looking at the data, the structure should be cross-validated on a new sample before it is treated as final.

**14. What additional information would you want before a final decision?**
For example: cross-validation on a new sample, item wording and theory, modification indices and residuals, reliability (omega/alpha), whether the data are ordinal (consider ordered estimation, e.g. WLSMV), and sample-size adequacy.

# Summary of Important Lessons

- CFA tests a pre-specified measurement model; EFA explores.
- A model must be identified (df ≥ 0) before it can be estimated; df > 0 is needed to test fit.
- Marker and variance-standardization methods give the same fit.
- Judge fit by the pattern of chi-square, CFI, TLI, RMSEA (and SRMR), not one number.
- Compare nested/alternative models (one-factor, two-factor, second-order) on both fit and theory.
